analysis.one_liner: Bars private gun sales at gun shows unless the seller is a licensed dealer.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime for anyone who is not a licensed gun dealer to sell or hand over a firearm at a gun show. Sales at a gun show would have to go through a licensed dealer, who under existing law runs a federal background check on the buyer. The ban would cover the whole event grounds, including parking lots, and violations would carry fines of $10,000 per gun involved and one to two years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who attend or live near gun shows, since every sale would run through a licensed dealer's background check rather than a private handshake sale with no check at all. Communities affected by gun violence would gain a closed avenue for sales to buyers who cannot pass a background check.

how_it_helps.text: At gun shows today, private sellers who are not licensed dealers can sell firearms without running the federal background check that licensed dealers must run, a gap often called the gun show loophole.
The bill makes it unlawful for anyone but a licensed dealer to transfer a firearm at a gun show, so every sale at the event would go through a dealer and its background-check process.
The ban covers the entire event premises, including parking areas, so sellers could not simply move transactions to the parking lot to avoid it.
Violations carry a fine of $10,000 multiplied by the number of firearms involved, one to two years in prison, or both, giving the rule teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Private collectors and hobbyists who sell guns at shows without a dealer license would have to stop selling directly or become licensed. Gun show operators and private sellers would lose the informal side of the market. Buyers would pay dealer transfer fees and wait for background checks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private gun sellers and casual collectors

drawbacks.text: The penalty is steep and applies per firearm: a private seller who transferred a handful of guns without a license could face fines of tens of thousands of dollars plus prison time, even for sales to an otherwise lawful buyer.
The bill only covers gun shows. Private sales arranged online, at a person's home, or elsewhere would remain outside this rule, so much of the private-sale market would be untouched.
Casual collectors and family hobbyists would face new costs: they would need to become licensed dealers or pay a licensed dealer to handle each sale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it closes the best-known version of the background-check gap at the exact venues where private, no-check sales are concentrated. The costs fall on a relatively small group, private sellers and hobbyists, and the stiff per-gun penalties are a blunt tool that some would call overbroad for casual sellers. The bigger limitation is coverage: it addresses gun shows only and leaves other private sales alone, so it is a partial fix rather than a universal background-check law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green of Texas introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the new Congress.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and then to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security the same day.
That was the last action of any kind. In two years the committee held no hearing, reported no bill text, and the full House never voted on it.
The bill had 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 429 voting members of the House at the time, and no Republican signed on.
Its Democratic co-sponsor count was modest even though Democrats held the House majority and controlled the Judiciary Committee that would have moved it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private, no-check gun sales at gun shows continued unchanged, and opponents of expanded background checks avoided any vote on the record. Licensed dealers lost the chance to become the exclusive channel for gun-show sales.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private gun sellers and check opponents

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the 116th Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Controlled whether the bill got a hearing or a floor vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the crime subcommittee on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or committee vote in two years.

against.name: Gun rights advocacy organizations, led by the NRA
against.role: Outside opposition to expanded background checks
against.what_they_did: Long opposed extending background checks to private gun sales, including at gun shows, and pressured lawmakers against such bills.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill died in committee without any vote that would have shown where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill would make licensed dealers the only legal channel for gun-show sales, locking in their gatekeeper role and giving them a new stream of transfer-fee business. It imposes no new rules on them and gives them an exclusive franchise over a market they currently share with private sellers.

industries.industry: Private gun sellers and casual collectors
industries.note: They could no longer sell directly at gun shows, including parking-lot sales, without a dealer license. Buyers facing a background check they cannot pass are the main losers of this change, which is the point of the bill.
The informal, no-check side of gun-show commerce, which draws many sellers and attendees, would be eliminated; operators could see fewer vendors and lower attendance.

A closed gun-show channel could modestly reduce sales to buyers who fail background checks, but manufacturers' sales run overwhelmingly through licensed dealers already, so the effect is small either way.
